# MANDATE

> ENS subnames are revocable powers of attorney for AI agents. Arc is where they spend. A company issues each of its AI agents an ENS subname whose resolver records are that agent's entire spending authority — budget, per-transaction cap, allowlisted recipients, and an expiry. The agent can read its own limits; it cannot edit them. Revoking the name refuses the agent's very next payment, before it signs, and again on-chain if it somehow tried.

MANDATE is built on three planes: authority (ENSv2 on Sepolia), enforcement (an off-chain service called the Enforcer, which watches Sepolia and compiles each mandate into a Privy conditional wallet policy and a signed Arc anchor — it can only ever narrow permission, never widen it), and money (Arc, where USDC is gas and every spend is checked against the anchor). Agents never hold private keys directly; their wallets are Privy-managed signers gated by policy.

## Docs

- [How MANDATE works](https://runmandate.xyz/docs): The three-plane model end to end, plus how to actually use the app — self-serve org onboarding through a gated wizard, registering an agent, revoking it.
- [ENS subnames as agent permissions](https://runmandate.xyz/docs/ens): Why a mandate is an ENSv2 subname with specific roles withheld — soulbound (no transfer-admin), self-expiring (no renew), narrowing-only sub-delegation.
- [Privy wallet policies, and their limits](https://runmandate.xyz/docs/privy): What Privy's conditional policies enforce for an agent's spending, and why their limits (private to one app, ~10 rolling aggregations, post-hoc updates) still need an onchain ledger alongside them.
- [Arc: USDC-gas payments for agents](https://runmandate.xyz/docs/arc): The org treasury as a revolving USDC credit facility on Arc, and how ERC-8004 identity/reputation and ERC-8183 job escrow compose into it.
- [Architecture](https://runmandate.xyz/docs/architecture): The authority/enforcement/money split in full, and what changed from the original single-chain design.
- [Security model and known limitations](https://runmandate.xyz/docs/security): The threat model, the Enforcer's own trust assumptions, and every known limitation disclosed rather than hidden — including where Privy's own chain authorization currently stops short.
- [Roadmap](https://runmandate.xyz/docs/roadmap): What this version deliberately leaves out — agent-to-agent commerce via ERC-8183 jobs, sub-delegation in the UI, wallet-ownership quorums as a first-class step.

## Optional

- [Source (GitHub)](https://github.com/victor-okpukpan/mandate): Full implementation — contracts, Enforcer, dashboard, agent runtimes.
